CausalChain: Chronic liver stress and oncogenic signaling -> Upregulation of m6A methyltransferases -> Aberrant m6A modification on tumor‐suppressive lncRNAs (e.g., MEG3) -> Altered lncRNA secondary structure -> Impaired binding to epigenetic regulators (EZH2, DNMTs) -> Derepression of metabolic and proliferative oncogenic pathways -> Enhanced HCC progression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), persistent chronic liver stress combined with oncogenic signaling leads to the overexpression of m6A methyltransferases, which in turn aberrantly modify tumor-suppressive lncRNAs such as MEG3. This excessive m6A deposition alters the secondary structure of these lncRNAs, thereby diminishing their capacity to bind epigenetic regulators (EZH2, DNMTs) essential for the repression of metabolic and proliferative pathways. The consequent loss of epigenetic control facilitates oncogenic activation and HCC progression. To counteract this cascade, we propose a dual-pronged methodology that exploits the precision of CRISPR-dCas13-mediated RNA editing to restore normal m6A patterns, and SHAPE-MaP coupled with in vitro RNA-binding assays to validate the restoration of lncRNA structure and function. This refined hypothesis not only adheres to the original causal chain but further addresses potential feedback loops and compensatory mechanisms, thereby enhancing its experimental testability and therapeutic relevance.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has been linked to aberrant epitranscriptomic regulation, yet the detailed mechanisms remain underexplored. We propose that chronic liver stress and oncogenic signaling stimulate the upregulation of m6A methyltransferases, resulting in excessive m6A modification of tumor‐suppressive long noncoding RNAs (such as MEG3). These modifications induce conformational changes in lncRNAs that impair their binding to critical epigenetic regulators (e.g., EZH2 and DNMTs), leading to a failure in repressing metabolic and proliferative oncogenic pathways. In this refined model, we integrate advanced CRISPR-dCas13 RNA editing technologies to selectively normalize m6A marks, with follow-up validation using SHAPE-MaP for RNA structural profiling and in vitro binding assays. This approach not only bolsters the causal link between m6A dysregulation and oncogenic signaling in HCC but also provides a robust experimental framework to assess the potential reversibility of lncRNA dysfunction, thereby outlining a novel therapeutic strategy.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that chronic liver stress and oncogenic signaling induce upregulation of m6A methyltransferases, leading to aberrant modification of tumor-suppressive lncRNAs, altered secondary structure, impaired binding to key epigenetic regulators, and HCC progression—with therapeutic reversal via CRISPR-dCas13 RNA editing and SHAPE-MaP validation. The revised hypothesis explicitly reinforces each step of this causal chain, introducing additional experimental validations such as in vitro binding assays and addressing potential compensatory feedback mechanisms. It also expands on the therapeutic approach by emphasizing a rigorous, technology-driven framework that leverages contemporary RNA editing and structural profiling techniques to directly test and potentially reverse the pathological epigenetic alterations in HCC.
